Telemachus defends the bard's freedom to please as his mind moves him, asserting that singers are not to blame (for their subject matter).

lines.original: αἴτιοι, ἀλλά ποθι Ζεὺς αἴτιος, ὅς τε δίδωσιν
lines.english: The bards are not to blame, but rather Zeus is to blame, who gives to each man as he wills.
lines.gloss:
**Key words:** αἴτιοι (nominative plural adjective from αἴτιος) "responsible, to blame"; Ζεύς (nominative singular) "Zeus"; αἴτιος (nominative singular adjective) "responsible, the cause"; δίδωσιν (3rd singular present active indicative of δίδωμι) "gives, grants." 

The line asserts that singers are not to blame (for how their songs affect listeners), but rather Zeus is responsible, who gives to toiling men as he wishes.

lines.original: ἀνδράσιν ἀλφηστῇσιν, ὅπως ἐθέλῃσιν, ἑκάστῳ.
lines.english: to men who labor for bread, to each one however he wishes.
lines.gloss:
**ἀνδράσιν** (noun, dative plural masculine of ἀνήρ): "to men" — dative of indirect object.

**ἀλφηστῇσιν** (noun, dative plural masculine of ἀλφηστής): "to grain-eaters, bread-winners" — an epithet for mortals, in apposition to ἀνδράσιν.

**ὅπως** (adverb): "as, however" — introduces manner.

**ἐθέλῃσιν** (verb, 3rd singular present subjunctive active of ἐθέλω): "he wishes" — subject is Zeus from the previous line.

**ἑκάστῳ** (adjective, dative singular masculine of ἕκαστος): "to each one" — emphasizing individual allocation.

Zeus distributes fate to mor

lines.original: τούτῳ δʼ οὐ νέμεσις Δαναῶν κακὸν οἶτον ἀείδειν·
lines.english: There is no blame in this man singing the sad fate of the Danaans.
lines.gloss: **Odyssey 1.348**: τούτῳ (dative singular of οὗτος, "for this one"), δʼ (postpositive particle δέ, "and/but"), οὐ νέμεσις (nominative singular noun, "it is not blame/resentment"), Δαναῶν (genitive plural of Δαναοί, "of the Danaans"), κακὸν οἶτον (accusative singular phrase, "evil fate/doom"), ἀείδειν (present active infinitive of ἀείδω, "to sing"). Penelope concedes it is no cause for blame that the bard sings the grievous doom of the Danaans.

lines.original: τὴν γὰρ ἀοιδὴν μᾶλλον ἐπικλείουσʼ ἄνθρωποι,
lines.english: For men praise most that song which comes newest to their ears.
lines.gloss:
**Key words:** 
- **τὴν** (accusative singular feminine, demonstrative pronoun): "that" (referring to the song)
- **ἀοιδὴν** (accusative singular, ἀοιδή): "song, lay"
- **μᾶλλον** (adverb, comparative of μάλα): "more, rather"
- **ἐπικλείουσι** (3rd plural present indicative, ἐπικλείω): "they praise, celebrate, acclaim"
- **ἄνθρωποι** (nominative plural, ἄνθρωπος): "people, men"

**Gloss:** Penelope justifies why audiences prefer songs about recent events: people praise most highly that song which comes newest to their ears.

lines.original: ἥ τις ἀκουόντεσσι νεωτάτη ἀμφιπέληται.
lines.english: whichever song comes newest to those who are listening.
lines.gloss:
**ἥ τις** (ἥ τις): indefinite relative pronoun, nominative singular feminine, "whichever" or "whatever (song)."
**ἀκουόντεσσι** (ἀκούοντες): present active participle of ἀκούω, dative plural masculine, "for those hearing/listening."
**νεωτάτη** (νέος): superlative adjective, nominative singular feminine, "newest" or "most recent."
**ἀμφιπέληται** (ἀμφιπέλομαι): present middle indicative, 3rd singular, "goes about" or "circulates among."

The line states that people most praise whichever song circulates most recently among listeners.

lines.original: σοὶ δʼ ἐπιτολμάτω κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀκούειν·
lines.english: Let your heart and spirit be bold to hear this.
lines.gloss:
**σοί** (dat. 2nd sg. of σύ) "to you"; **ἐπιτολμάτω** (3rd sg. pres. impv. of ἐπιτολμάω) "let it dare"; **κραδίη** (nom. sg.) "heart"; **θυμός** (nom. sg.) "spirit"; **ἀκούειν** (pres. inf. of ἀκούω) "to hear/listen." 

The line urges the listener (Penelope) to let her heart and spirit be bold enough to hear what follows—namely, that Odysseus was not alone in losing his homecoming.

lines.original: οὐ γὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς οἶος ἀπώλεσε νόστιμον ἦμαρ
lines.english: For Odysseus was not the only one to lose his day of homecoming.
lines.gloss:
**Key words:** Ὀδυσσεὺς (nom. sg., "Odysseus"), οἶος (nom. sg. adj., "alone"), ἀπώλεσε (3rd sg. aor. act. ind. of ἀπόλλυμι, "lost/destroyed"), νόστιμον (acc. sg. adj., "of return/homecoming"), ἦμαρ (acc. sg. neut., "day"). 

The line states that Odysseus was not the only one who lost his day of homecoming, contextualizing his suffering within the broader tragedy of the Trojan War.

lines.original: ἐν Τροίῃ, πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ ἄλλοι φῶτες ὄλοντο.
lines.english: in Troy, and many other men perished too.
lines.gloss: **Τροίῃ** (noun, dat. sg. fem.): "in Troy" (locative dative); **πολλοὶ** (adj., nom. pl. masc.): "many"; **ἄλλοι** (adj., nom. pl. masc.): "other"; **φῶτες** (noun, nom. pl. masc.): "men"; **ὄλοντο** (verb, 3rd pl. aor. mid. ind. of ὄλλυμι): "perished, died." The speaker emphasizes that Odysseus was not alone in losing his homecoming day at Troy—many other men also perished there.

lines.original: ἀλλʼ εἰς οἶκον ἰοῦσα τὰ σʼ αὐτῆς ἔργα κόμιζε,
lines.english: But go into the house and see to your own tasks
lines.gloss:
**ἀλλʼ εἰς οἶκον ἰοῦσα τὰ σʼ αὐτῆς ἔργα κόμιζε,**

**ἰοῦσα**: present participle feminine nominative singular of εἶμι, "going"; **σʼ αὐτῆς**: crasis of σά (possessive adjective "your") + αὐτῆς (genitive feminine singular "of yourself/your own"), forming "your own"; **ἔργα**: neuter plural accusative of ἔργον, "works, tasks"; **κόμιζε**: present imperative 2nd singular of κομίζω, "attend to, take care of." This is the formulaic dismissal telling a woman to return home and occupy herself with her own domestic tasks.

lines.original: ἱστόν τʼ ἠλακάτην τε, καὶ ἀμφιπόλοισι κέλευε
lines.english: the loom and the distaff, and command your handmaids
lines.gloss: **ἱστόν** (acc. sg. masc., ἱστός) "loom"; **ἠλακάτην** (acc. sg. fem., ἠλακάτη) "distaff"; **ἀμφιπόλοισι** (dat. pl. fem., ἀμφίπολος) "handmaidens, serving women"; **κέλευε** (2nd sg. pres. imperat., κελεύω) "command, bid." Telemachus instructs Penelope to attend to traditional women's work—the loom and distaff—and to give orders to her servants, asserting male authority over public speech.

lines.original: ἔργον ἐποίχεσθαι· μῦθος δʼ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει
lines.english: To attend to their work; but speech will be the concern of men, especially mine, for mine is the power in this house.
lines.gloss:
**ἔργον ἐποίχεσθαι· μῦθος δʼ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει**

**ἔργον** (noun, acc. sg. neut.): "work," object of ἐποίχεσθαι. **ἐποίχεσθαι** (verb, pres. mid./pass. inf.): "to attend to, go about," complementary infinitive with κέλευε from the previous line. **μῦθος** (noun, nom. sg. masc.): "speech, tale," subject of μελήσει. **ἄνδρεσσι** (noun, dat. pl. masc.): "to/for men," dative of interest with μελήσει. **μελήσει** (verb, fut. 3rd sg.): "will be

lines.original: πᾶσι, μάλιστα δʼ ἐμοί· τοῦ γὰρ κράτος ἔστʼ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ.
lines.english: All men, but especially to me, for mine is the power in this house.
lines.gloss: **πᾶσι** (πᾶς): dative plural masculine adjective, "to all" or "for all [men]," referring to the men just mentioned. **μάλιστα** (μάλιστα): adverb (superlative of μάλα), "especially" or "most of all." **ἐμοί** (ἐγώ): dative singular pronoun, "to me" or "for me." **κράτος** (κράτος): nominative singular neuter noun, "power" or "authority." **οἴκῳ** (οἶκος): dative singular masculine noun, "in the house/household." Telemachus asserts that the matter concerns all the men, but especially himself, since the power/authority in the house is his.

lines.original: μητρὸς ἐμῆς μνηστῆρες ὑπέρβιον ὕβριν ἔχοντες,
lines.english: The suitors of my mother, possessing outrageous insolence,
lines.gloss: **μητρὸς** (gen. sing. fem. of μήτηρ, "of mother") and **μνηστῆρες** (nom. pl. masc. of μνηστήρ, "suitors") frame the line. **ὑπέρβιον** (acc. sing. fem. of ὑπέρβιος, "excessive, outrageous") modifies **ὕβριν** (acc. sing. fem. of ὕβρις, "violence, insolence"), while **ἔχοντες** (pres. act. part. nom. pl. masc. of ἔχω, "having, displaying") describes the suitors' conduct. The line describes the suitors of Telemachus's mother as displaying excessive outrage.

lines.original: νῦν μὲν δαινύμενοι τερπώμεθα, μηδὲ βοητὺς
lines.english: Now let us feast and take our pleasure, and let there be no shouting.
lines.gloss: **νῦν** (adverb): "now," temporal marker. **δαινύμενοι** (present middle participle, nominative plural masculine, from *δαίνυμι*): "feasting," "banqueting." **τερπώμεθα** (present middle subjunctive, 1st plural, from *τέρπω*): "let us take pleasure," hortatory subjunctive. **βοητὺς** (noun, nominative singular feminine): "shouting," "outcry." Telemachus urges the suitors to enjoy feasting in peace without clamor, temporarily setting aside conflict to appreciate the bard's performance.

lines.original: ἔστω, ἐπεὶ τόδε καλὸν ἀκουέμεν ἐστὶν ἀοιδοῦ
lines.english: Let there be no shouting, since it is fine to listen to the singer.
lines.gloss: **ἔστω** (3rd sg. pres. imperat. of εἰμί): "let there be" – imperative following the prohibition in the previous line. **ἐπεί**: "since, because" (causal conjunction) introduces the rationale. **καλόν** (neut. sg. nom., predicate adjective): "noble, fine" – substantive with ἐστιν in the epexegetic infinitive construction. **ἀκουέμεν** (pres. inf. of ἀκούω): "to listen to" (+ gen. ἀοιδοῦ). **ἀοιδοῦ** (gen. sg. of ἀοιδός): "of the bard" – objective genitive with the infinitive. The speaker argues that listening to such a singer is a noble thing.

lines.original: τοιοῦδʼ οἷος ὅδʼ ἐστί, θεοῖς ἐναλίγκιος αὐδήν.
lines.english: Such as this man is, like the gods in voice.
lines.gloss:
**τοιοῦδʼ** (τοιοῦδε) – demonstrative pronoun, genitive singular masculine, "such as this," depending on ἀοιδοῦ from the previous line. **οἷος** – relative pronoun, nominative singular masculine, "such as," introducing a qualitative clause. **ἐναλίγκιος** – adjective, nominative singular masculine, "like, resembling," modifying the subject (the bard). **αὐδήν** – noun, accusative singular feminine, "in voice," indicating respect of resemblance.

The line praises a bard of this quality, who is like the gods in voice.

lines.original: ἠῶθεν δʼ ἀγορήνδε καθεζώμεσθα κιόντες
lines.english: At dawn let us go and sit down in assembly.
lines.gloss: **ἠῶθεν** (adverb): "at dawn," "early in the morning," temporal adverb indicating the time of the proposed action. **ἀγορήνδε** (adverb): "to the assembly," directional adverb with -δε suffix showing motion toward the place of gathering. **καθεζώμεσθα** (verb): 1st plural aorist middle subjunctive of καθέζομαι, "let us sit down," hortatory subjunctive. **κιόντες** (participle): nominative plural masculine aorist participle of κίω, "having gone" or "going," indicating manner or attendant circumstance. The speaker proposes that at dawn they go and sit down in assembly.

lines.original: πάντες, ἵνʼ ὕμιν μῦθον ἀπηλεγέως ἀποείπω,
lines.english: all of you, so that I may declare my word to you bluntly
lines.gloss: **πάντες** (adj. nom. pl. masc., "all [of you]") addresses the suitors collectively; **ἵνα** (conj., "so that") introduces a purpose clause; **μῦθον** (noun acc. sg., "my word/speech") is the object of **ἀποείπω** (verb 1st sg. aor. subj. act., "I may declare/pronounce"); **ἀπηλεγέως** (adv., "relentlessly, bluntly") modifies the declaration. Telemachus demands that all the suitors gather so he may deliver his uncompromising message to them.

lines.original: ἐξιέναι μεγάρων· ἄλλας δʼ ἀλεγύνετε δαῖτας,
lines.english: Leave my halls and prepare other feasts, consuming your own goods, visiting house by house.
lines.gloss:
**ἐξιέναι** (infinitive, present active of ἔξειμι): "to go out, depart" — the imperatival infinitive commanding the suitors' departure. **μεγάρων** (genitive plural, neuter noun μέγαρον): "from the halls" — marking separation. **ἄλλας** (accusative plural feminine, adjective ἄλλος): "other" — modifying δαῖτας. **ἀλεγύνετε** (2nd plural present imperative, ἀλεγύνω): "prepare, arrange" — commanding the suitors to organize their own feasts. **δαῖτας** (accusative plural feminine, δαίς): "feasts, banquets" — direct object of ἀλεγύνετε.

Telemachus commands the suitors to leave his halls and prepare their

lines.original: ὑμὰ κτήματʼ ἔδοντες, ἀμειβόμενοι κατὰ οἴκους.
lines.english: eating your own possessions, taking turns feasting from house to house.
lines.gloss: **ὑμά** (possessive adj., neuter acc. pl.) "your own"; **κτήματ(α)** (noun, neut. acc. pl.) "possessions, goods"; **ἔδοντες** (pres. part., nom. pl. masc. of ἔδω) "eating, consuming"; **ἀμειβόμενοι** (pres. mid. part., nom. pl. masc. of ἀμείβω) "alternating, taking turns"; **κατὰ οἴκους** (prep. + acc. pl.) "from house to house." Telemachus challenges the suitors: if it seems better to consume your own possessions, going in turn from house to house.

lines.original: εἰ δʼ ὕμιν δοκέει τόδε λωίτερον καὶ ἄμεινον
lines.english: But if this seems to you more profitable and better
lines.gloss:
**εἰ δʼ ὕμιν δοκέει τόδε λωίτερον καὶ ἄμεινον**

*εἰ* (conj.) "if"; *ὕμιν* (dat. pl. of σύ) "to you"; *δοκέει* (3rd sg. pres. indic. of δοκέω) "it seems"; *λωίτερον* (neut. comp. adj.) "more desirable, preferable"; *ἄμεινον* (neut. comp. adj. of ἀγαθός) "better." Telemachus presents a conditional: "But if this seems to you more desirable and better..."

lines.original: ἔμμεναι, ἀνδρὸς ἑνὸς βίοτον νήποινον ὀλέσθαι,
lines.english: that one man's livelihood should be destroyed without recompense
lines.gloss:
**ἔμμεναι** (pres. inf. of εἰμί) "to be" — completes the indirect statement begun in the previous line. **ἀνδρὸς ἑνὸς** (gen. sg. masc.) "of one man" — partitive genitive with βίοτον. **βίοτον** (acc. sg. masc.) "livelihood, property" — subject of the infinitive ὀλέσθαι. **νήποινον** (acc. sg. masc.) "unavenged, without compensation" — predicative adjective. **ὀλέσθαι** (aor. inf. mid. of ὄλλυμι) "to be destroyed, to perish" — complementary infinitive completing ἔμμεναι.

The line means: "that the livelihood of one man should perish unavenged

lines.original: κείρετʼ· ἐγὼ δὲ θεοὺς ἐπιβώσομαι αἰὲν ἐόντας,
lines.english: Go ahead and plunder; but I will call upon the everlasting gods.
lines.gloss:
**κείρετʼ·** κείρω, 2nd pl. pres. mid. imperative, "shear (for yourselves)," "cut," "plunder." **ἐγὼ** 1st sg. personal pronoun, nominative, "I." **ἐπιβώσομαι** ἐπιβοάω, 1st sg. fut. mid. indicative, "I will call upon," "invoke." **αἰὲν** adverb, "always," "ever." **ἐόντας** εἰμί, pres. participle masc. acc. pl., "being," modifying θεούς.

The speaker tells others to keep plundering while asserting he will invoke the eternal gods as witnesses or avengers.

lines.original: αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς δῷσι παλίντιτα ἔργα γενέσθαι·
lines.english: in hope that Zeus may grant that deeds of requital come to pass
lines.gloss:
**αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς δῷσι παλίντιτα ἔργα γενέσθαι·**

**αἴ κέ** (conditional particle + modal particle) "if perhaps"; **Ζεύς** (nom. sg.) "Zeus"; **δῷσι** (3rd sg. aor. subj. of δίδωμι) "should grant/give"; **παλίντιτα** (acc. pl. neut. of παλίντιτος) "requiting, retaliatory"; **γενέσθαι** (aor. inf. of γίγνομαι) "to happen, come to pass." Odysseus invokes the possibility that Zeus might grant retributive deeds against the suitors.

lines.original: νήποινοί κεν ἔπειτα δόμων ἔντοσθεν ὄλοισθε.
lines.english: You would then perish within the halls unavenged.
lines.gloss:
**νήποινοί** (νήποινος, -ον, nominative plural masculine): "unavenged, without penalty," modifying the understood subject (the suitors). **κεν** (ἄν, modal particle): marks the potential mood with the optative. **ἔπειτα** (adverb): "then, thereafter." **ὄλοισθε** (ὄλλυμι, 2nd plural aorist middle optative): "you would perish/be destroyed."

Odysseus warns that the suitors would then perish unavenged within the halls, suggesting their death would be justified and go unpunished.

lines.original: Τηλέμαχʼ, ἦ μάλα δή σε διδάσκουσιν θεοὶ αὐτοὶ
lines.english: Telemakhos, surely the gods themselves are teaching you
lines.gloss:
**Τηλέμαχʼ, ἦ μάλα δή σε διδάσκουσιν θεοὶ αὐτοὶ**

*Τηλέμαχʼ* (voc. sg., "Telemachus"); *ἦ* (particle, "truly, indeed"); *διδάσκουσιν* (3rd pl. pres. act. indic., διδάσκω, "they teach"); *θεοὶ* (nom. pl., "the gods"); *αὐτοὶ* (nom. pl. masc., intensive, "themselves"). Antinous ironically remarks that the gods themselves are teaching Telemachus to be bold and speak confidently before the assembly.

lines.original: ὑψαγόρην τʼ ἔμεναι καὶ θαρσαλέως ἀγορεύειν·
lines.english: to be lofty in speech and to speak boldly.
lines.gloss:
**Gloss for Odyssey 1.386:**

ὑψαγόρην (accusative singular adjective, modifying an implied subject "you") = "high-speaking, lofty in speech"; τʼ (enclitic particle) = "and"; ἔμεναι (present infinitive of εἰμί) = "to be"; θαρσαλέως (adverb) = "boldly, confidently"; ἀγορεύειν (present infinitive) = "to speak." The line continues the thought that the gods themselves teach Telemachus to be lofty in speech and to speak boldly in the assembly.

lines.original: μὴ σέ γʼ ἐν ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ βασιλῆα Κρονίων
lines.english: May Zeus son of Kronos not make you king in sea-girt Ithaka
lines.gloss:
**Key words:** μή (negative particle) with σέ (accusative singular of σύ, "you"); ἀμφιάλῳ (adjective, dative singular feminine, "sea-girt"); Ἰθάκῃ (dative singular, "in Ithaca"); βασιλῆα (accusative singular, "king"); Κρονίων (nominative singular, "son of Kronos" = Zeus).

Athena (as Mentes) expresses the wish that Zeus may make Telemachus king in sea-girt Ithaca, introducing a prayer for his future sovereignty.

lines.original: ποιήσειεν, ὅ τοι γενεῇ πατρώιόν ἐστιν.
lines.english: may he make you king, which is yours by ancestral right.
lines.gloss:
**ποιήσειεν, ὅ τοι γενεῇ πατρώιόν ἐστιν.**

**ποιήσειεν** (3rd sg. aorist optative active, ποιέω): "may he make" or "would make" – expresses a wish that Cronus's son Zeus might make [you king]. **ὅ** (neut. nom. sg. relative pronoun): "which (thing)," introducing a relative clause. **γενεῇ** (dat. sg., γενεή): "by birth" or "by lineage" – dative of respect. **πατρώιόν** (neut. nom. sg. adj., πατρῷος): "ancestral," "paternal," modifying the implied kingship that is hereditary in your family line.

lines.original: Ἀντίνοʼ, ἦ καί μοι νεμεσήσεαι ὅττι κεν εἴπω;
lines.english: Antinous, will you truly be angry with me for whatever I may say?
lines.gloss: **Ἀντίνοʼ** (Antinoe, vocative) - "Antinous"; **νεμεσήσεαι** (νεμεσάω, 2nd sg. future middle indicative) - "will you be indignant/angry"; **ὅττι** (relative pronoun, neuter accusative) - "at whatever" or "because"; **κεν** (particle) - modal particle with subjunctive, "might"; **εἴπω** (λέγω/εἶπον, 1st sg. aorist subjunctive) - "I say/speak". Telemachus addresses Antinous, asking if he will be angry at whatever he is about to say.

lines.original: καί κεν τοῦτʼ ἐθέλοιμι Διός γε διδόντος ἀρέσθαι.
lines.english: I would even be willing to take this for myself if Zeus should grant it.
lines.gloss: **καί** (adv.): "even," intensive; **ἐθέλοιμι** (1st sg. pres. opt. act., ἐθέλω): "I would be willing"; **Διός** (gen. sg., Ζεύς): "of Zeus," genitive absolute construction; **διδόντος** (pres. part. gen. sg. masc., δίδωμι): "giving," agreeing with Διός; **ἀρέσθαι** (aor. inf. mid., ἀραρίσκω): "to take up, accept." The speaker declares willingness to accept "this" (τοῦτο) even if Zeus were granting it.

lines.original: ἦ φῂς τοῦτο κάκιστον ἐν ἀνθρώποισι τετύχθαι;
lines.english: Do you really say this is the worst thing that has happened among mortals?
lines.gloss: **φῂς** (φημί, 2nd sg. pres. ind. act.) "you say"; **κάκιστον** (κακός, superlative neut. sg. nom./acc.) "worst"; **ἀνθρώποισι** (ἄνθρωπος, dat. pl.) "among men"; **τετύχθαι** (τεύχω, perf. inf. mid./pass.) "to have been made/to be." Telemachus challenges: "Do you say this (kingship) has been made the worst thing among men?"

lines.original: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι κακὸν βασιλευέμεν· αἶψά τέ οἱ δῶ
lines.english: For it is not at all a bad thing to be a king; quickly his house becomes wealthy and he himself more honored.
lines.gloss:
**οὐ μὲν γάρ τι κακὸν βασιλευέμεν· αἶψά τέ οἱ δῶ**

*κακὸν* (adj. nom. sg. neut.): "evil, bad thing"; *βασιλευέμεν* (pres. inf.): "to be king, to rule"; *αἶψα* (adv.): "quickly, straightway"; *δῶ* (noun nom. sg. neut.): "house, palace." The speaker asserts that kingship is not an evil thing, for quickly one's house becomes wealthy (continuation in next line).

lines.original: ἀφνειὸν πέλεται καὶ τιμηέστερος αὐτός.
lines.english: His house grows wealthy and he himself becomes more honored.
lines.gloss:
**ἀφνειὸν** (adjective, nominative singular neuter) "wealthy, rich" - modifies δῶ (house) from the previous line. **πέλεται** (verb, 3rd singular present middle indicative, πέλω) "becomes, is." **τιμηέστερος** (adjective, comparative nominative singular masculine) "more honored, more esteemed" - from τίμιος. **αὐτός** (pronoun, nominative singular masculine) "he himself" - refers to the king. 

The line describes the benefits of kingship: the king's house becomes wealthy and he himself becomes more honored.

lines.original: ἀλλʼ ἦ τοι βασιλῆες Ἀχαιῶν εἰσὶ καὶ ἄλλοι
lines.english: But indeed there are other kings of the Achaeans as well
lines.gloss:
**ἀλλʼ ἦ τοι βασιλῆες Ἀχαιῶν εἰσὶ καὶ ἄλλοι**

**βασιλῆες** (nom. pl. masc., βασιλεύς) "kings"; **Ἀχαιῶν** (gen. pl., Ἀχαιοί) "of the Achaeans"; **εἰσί** (3rd pl. pres. indic., εἰμί) "are"; **ἄλλοι** (nom. pl. masc., ἄλλος) "others." "But indeed there are also other kings of the Achaeans," acknowledging the presence of multiple basileis beyond the speaker.

lines.original: πολλοὶ ἐν ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ, νέοι ἠδὲ παλαιοί,
lines.english: Many in sea-girt Ithaca, both young and old.
lines.gloss: **πολλοί** (adj. nom. pl. masc.) "many" - modifying the understood "kings" from the previous line. **ἀμφιάλῳ** (adj. dat. sg. fem.) "sea-girt, surrounded by sea" - epithet modifying Ἰθάκῃ. **Ἰθάκῃ** (noun dat. sg. fem.) "in Ithaca" - locative dative. **νέοι** (adj. nom. pl. masc.) "young (men)" and **παλαιοί** (adj. nom. pl. masc.) "old (men)" - contrasting pair describing the many kings/nobles present on the island.

lines.original: τῶν κέν τις τόδʼ ἔχῃσιν, ἐπεὶ θάνε δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
lines.english: One of them might have this, since godlike Odysseus is dead.
lines.gloss:
**τῶν** (gen. pl. demonstrative pronoun) "of these/them"; **κέν** (modal particle = ἄν) "would/might"; **ἔχῃσιν** (3rd sg. pres. subj. act. of ἔχω) "may have/possess"; **θάνε** (3rd sg. aor. act. of θνῄσκω) "died"; **δῖος** (nom. sg. masc. adj.) "godlike, noble."

"One of these (suitors) may have this (kingship), since godlike Odysseus has died"—Telemachus acknowledges the suitors' ambitions while asserting his own claim to the household.

lines.original: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν οἴκοιο ἄναξ ἔσομʼ ἡμετέροιο
lines.english: But I shall be master of our own house.
lines.gloss:
**Gloss for αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν οἴκοιο ἄναξ ἔσομʼ ἡμετέροιο:**

Key words: **αὐτάρ** (particle, "but, however"), **ἐγών** (pronoun, nominative 1st sg., "I"), **οἴκοιο** (noun, genitive sg. of οἶκος, "of the house"), **ἄναξ** (noun, nominative sg., "lord, master"), **ἔσομ(αι)** (verb, future 1st sg. of εἰμί, "I will be"), **ἡμετέροιο** (possessive adjective, genitive sg., "our"). Telemachus asserts his claim: "But I shall be master of our house."

lines.original: καὶ δμώων, οὕς μοι ληίσσατο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
lines.english: and of the slaves whom godlike Odysseus won for me.
lines.gloss:
**καὶ δμώων, οὕς μοι ληίσσατο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.**

δμώων (genitive plural of δμώς, "slave, servant") depends on ἄναξ in the previous line; οὕς (accusative plural masculine relative pronoun, "whom") is the object of ληίσσατο (3rd singular aorist middle indicative of ληίζομαι, "to take as booty, plunder"); δῖος (nominative singular masculine adjective, "divine, godly") modifies Ὀδυσσεύς as subject. The speaker claims lordship over the household and the slaves whom divine Odysseus seized as plunder.

lines.original: Τηλέμαχʼ, ἦ τοι ταῦτα θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται,
lines.english: Telemachos, truly these things lie in the laps of the gods.
lines.gloss:
**Τηλέμαχʼ, ἦ τοι ταῦτα θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται**

*Τηλέμαχʼ* (vocative, "Telemachus"); *ἦ τοι* (affirmative particle + particle, "truly indeed"); *ταῦτα* (neuter plural nominative demonstrative, "these things"); *γούνασι* (dative plural noun, "knees," metaphorically meaning "power/lap"); *κεῖται* (3rd singular present middle/passive, "lies/rests"). The speaker asserts that these matters rest in the lap of the gods, i.e., are under divine control.

lines.original: ὅς τις ἐν ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ βασιλεύσει Ἀχαιῶν·
lines.english: who among the Achaeans will be king in sea-girt Ithaca
lines.gloss: **ὅς** (relative pronoun, nominative singular masculine) "who/whoever"; **ἀμφιάλῳ** (adjective, dative singular feminine) "sea-girt, surrounded by sea"; **Ἰθάκῃ** (noun, dative singular) "Ithaca"; **βασιλεύσει** (verb, future indicative 3rd singular) "will rule, will be king"; **Ἀχαιῶν** (noun, genitive plural) "of the Achaeans." The line concerns whoever among the Achaeans will rule over sea-girt Ithaca, typically expressing uncertainty about future kingship.

lines.original: κτήματα δʼ αὐτὸς ἔχοις καὶ δώμασιν οἷσιν ἀνάσσοις.
lines.english: But may you keep your possessions and rule in your own house.
lines.gloss: **κτήματα** (neuter plural accusative from κτῆμα): "possessions, property" — direct object of ἔχοις. **ἔχοις** (2nd singular present optative active from ἔχω): "may you hold/possess" — expresses a wish. **δώμασιν** (neuter plural dative from δῶμα): "in your halls/palace" — dative of place where. **ἀνάσσοις** (2nd singular present optative active from ἀνάσσω): "may you rule/be lord" — another optative of wish, governing δώμασιν. The line expresses a wish that the addressee retain his possessions and sovereignty over his own household.

lines.original: μὴ γὰρ ὅ γʼ ἔλθοι ἀνὴρ ὅς τίς σʼ ἀέκοντα βίηφιν
lines.english: May no man come who by force against your will
lines.gloss:
**Key words:** *ἔλθοι* (aorist optative, 3rd singular of ἔρχομαι, "come") expresses a negative wish ("may he not come"); *ἀνήρ* (nominative singular, "man/husband") refers to Odysseus; *ἀέκοντα* (accusative singular masculine present participle of ἀέκων, "unwilling") modifies "you"; *βίηφιν* (dative singular, "by force/violence") indicates means. 

The speaker wishes that no man (Odysseus) should come who would compel you against your will by force.

lines.original: κτήματʼ ἀπορραίσει, Ἰθάκης ἔτι ναιετοώσης.
lines.english: will seize your possessions by force while you still dwell in Ithaca.
lines.gloss:
**κτήματʼ ἀπορραίσει, Ἰθάκης ἔτι ναιετοώσης.**

Key words: **κτήματα** (noun, neut. pl. acc.) "possessions, property"; **ἀπορραίσει** (verb, 3rd sing. fut. act. indic. of ἀπο-ῥαίω) "will tear away, plunder"; **Ἰθάκης** (noun, fem. gen. sing.) "of Ithaca"; **ναιετοώσης** (verb, fem. gen. sing. pres. act. participle of ναιετάω) "dwelling, inhabiting." The line warns against someone who would plunder possessions while Ithaca still stands/is inhabited.

lines.original: ἀλλʼ ἐθέλω σε, φέριστε, περὶ ξείνοιο ἐρέσθαι,
lines.english: But I want to ask you, my excellent friend, about the stranger.
lines.gloss:
**Target: ἀλλʼ ἐθέλω σε, φέριστε, περὶ ξείνοιο ἐρέσθαι,**

ἐθέλω (1st sg. pres. act. indic. of ἐθέλω): "I wish, I want"; φέριστε (voc. sg. masc. superl. of φέρτερος): "best one, excellent one"; περί + gen.: "concerning, about"; ξείνοιο (gen. sg. of ξεῖνος): "stranger, guest"; ἐρέσθαι (pres. mid./aor. mid. inf. of ἐρείρομαι/ἐρωτάω): "to ask, inquire." The speaker wishes to ask the addressee about a stranger/guest.

lines.original: ὁππόθεν οὗτος ἀνήρ, ποίης δʼ ἐξ εὔχεται εἶναι
lines.english: Where this man is from and from what land he claims to be.
lines.gloss:
**ὁππόθεν** (adverb): "from where, whence" – interrogative of origin introducing an indirect question. **οὗτος ἀνήρ** (demonstrative pronoun + noun, nom. sg. masc.): "this man" – subject of the indirect question. **ποίης** (interrogative adjective, gen. sg. fem.): "of what (land/people)" – genitive of source with **γαίης** understood. **ἐξ** (preposition + gen.): "from" – here governing the elided/understood noun. **εὔχεται** (verb, 3rd sg. pres. mid. indic., εὔχομαι): "he claims/boasts to be" – middle voice expressing personal claim about origin.

Telemachus asks about the stranger's origins: from where this man comes and from what land he claims to be.

lines.original: γαίης, ποῦ δέ νύ οἱ γενεὴ καὶ πατρὶς ἄρουρα.
lines.english: from what land, and where are his lineage and his native soil.
lines.gloss:
**γαίης** (γῆ, genitive singular, feminine): "of land, earth" — continues the question about the stranger's origins, dependent on ἐξ εὔχεται εἶναι from the previous line.

**ποῦ** (adverb): "where?" — introduces a direct question about location.

**γενεὴ** (γενεή, nominative singular, feminine): "lineage, family, birth" — one of two subjects in the question.

**πατρὶς** (πατρίς, nominative singular, feminine): "fatherland, native land" — second subject, paired with γενεή.

**ἄρουρα** (ἄρουρα, nominative singular, feminine): "plowland, field, country" — in apposition to πατρίς, emphasizing territorial origin.

The speaker asks from what land the stranger comes

lines.original: ἠέ τινʼ ἀγγελίην πατρὸς φέρει ἐρχομένοιο,
lines.english: Or does he bring some message of his father's coming,
lines.gloss:
**Odyssey 15.423** – ἠέ τινʼ ἀγγελίην πατρὸς φέρει ἐρχομένοιο

**ἠέ** (particle): "or" (disjunctive, continuing the indirect question). **ἀγγελίην** (fem. acc. sg., ἀγγελίη): "message, news" (object of φέρει). **φέρει** (3rd sg. pres. act. indic., φέρω): "does he bring." **ἐρχομένοιο** (masc. gen. sg. pres. mid. participle, ἔρχομαι): "coming, returning" (modifying πατρός). The speaker asks whether the stranger brings news of a father who is on his way home.

lines.original: ἦ ἑὸν αὐτοῦ χρεῖος ἐελδόμενος τόδʼ ἱκάνει;
lines.english: or does he come here seeking some need of his own that he desires?
lines.gloss:
**χρεῖος** (noun, accusative neuter singular) "need, business" — ἑὸν αὐτοῦ χρεῖος "his own business/affair." **ἐελδόμενος** (participle, present middle nominative masculine singular, from *ἔλδομαι*) "desiring, seeking." **ἱκάνει** (verb, 3rd singular present indicative, from *ἱκάνω/ἱκνέομαι*) "he comes, arrives." 

The line asks whether the stranger comes seeking to fulfill some personal need or business of his own.

lines.original: οἷον ἀναΐξας ἄφαρ οἴχεται, οὐδʼ ὑπέμεινε
lines.english: How he sprang up and left at once, nor did he wait
lines.gloss: **οἷον** (exclamatory adverb): "how!" or "what a way!" expressing astonishment. **ἀναΐξας** (aorist participle, nominative masculine singular, from ἀν-αΐσσω): "springing up," "leaping up." **ἄφαρ** (adverb): "straightway," "immediately." **οἴχεται** (3rd singular present middle/passive indicative, from οἴχομαι): "he has gone," "he is gone." **ὑπέμεινε** (3rd singular aorist indicative, from ὑπομένω): "he waited," "he remained." The line describes someone leaping up and departing immediately without waiting.

lines.original: γνώμεναι· οὐ μὲν γάρ τι κακῷ εἰς ὦπα ἐῴκει.
lines.english: for he did not look at all like a base man in appearance.
lines.gloss:
**γνώμεναι** (γιγνώσκω, aorist infinitive): "to learn, ascertain"; depends on ὑπέμεινε from the previous line. **κακῷ** (κακός, dative singular masculine/neuter): "evil, cowardly"; modifies an implied person. **ὦπα** (ὤψ, accusative singular): "face, appearance." **ἐῴκει** (ἔοικα, pluperfect): "he resembled, seemed like." 

The stranger did not wait to be recognized, for he did not at all resemble a coward in appearance.

lines.original: Εὐρύμαχʼ, ἦ τοι νόστος ἀπώλετο πατρὸς ἐμοῖο·
lines.english: Eurymachos, truly the homecoming of my father is lost.
lines.gloss:
**Εὐρύμαχʼ, ἦ τοι νόστος ἀπώλετο πατρὸς ἐμοῖο·**

*Εὐρύμαχ(ε)* (vocative): "Eurymachus," addressing one of the suitors. *ἦ τοι* (particle + particle): "truly, indeed," emphasizing the assertion. *νόστος* (nominative singular masculine): "homecoming, return." *ἀπώλετο* (3rd singular aorist middle indicative of ἀπόλλυμι): "has perished, is lost." *πατρός* (genitive singular masculine): "of father." Telemachus declares to Eurymachus that his father's return has truly been lost.

lines.original: οὔτʼ οὖν ἀγγελίῃ ἔτι πείθομαι, εἴ ποθεν ἔλθοι,
lines.english: I no longer trust any message, even if one should come from somewhere,
lines.gloss:
**οὔτʼ οὖν** (οὔτε + οὖν): "nor then/therefore" – conjunction combining negative correlation with inferential particle. **ἀγγελίῃ** (dat. sg. fem. of ἀγγελία): "message, news" – dative of means or object of trust. **πείθομαι** (1st sg. pres. mid./pass. indic. of πείθω): "I trust, believe in, am persuaded by" – middle voice expressing internal conviction. **εἴ...ἔλθοι** (3rd sg. aor. opt. of ἔρχομαι): "if it should come" – optative in remote future condition, expressing doubt about hypothetical arrival.

Telemachus declares he no longer trusts any message about his father, even if one should arrive from somewhere, showing his deep skepticism after years of

lines.original: οὔτε θεοπροπίης ἐμπάζομαι, ἥν τινα μήτηρ
lines.english: nor do I heed any prophecy that my mother might consult by summoning a seer to the hall.
lines.gloss:
**Key words:** θεοπροπίης (gen. sg. fem. of θεοπροπίη) "prophecy, oracle"; ἐμπάζομαι (1st sg. pres. mid. indic. of ἐμπάζομαι) "I heed, take notice of"; μήτηρ (nom. sg. fem.) "mother." 

Telemachus declares he does not heed any prophecy which his mother, summoning a seer into the hall, might inquire about.

lines.original: ἐς μέγαρον καλέσασα θεοπρόπον ἐξερέηται.
lines.english: having summoned a prophet to the hall to question him about it.
lines.gloss:
**ἐς μέγαρον καλέσασα θεοπρόπον ἐξερέηται.**

Key words: **καλέσασα** (aorist participle, feminine nominative singular of καλέω, "having summoned"), **θεοπρόπον** (accusative singular, "prophet, seer"), **ἐξερέηται** (present subjunctive, 3rd singular of ἐξερέομαι, "she might question"). Telemachus dismisses the prophet his mother might summon to the hall for consultation, expressing skepticism about prophecy in response to his mother's religious practices.

lines.original: ξεῖνος δʼ οὗτος ἐμὸς πατρώιος ἐκ Τάφου ἐστίν,
lines.english: This stranger of mine is a family friend from Taphos.
lines.gloss: **ξεῖνος** (nom. sg. masc., "guest-friend") serves as the subject; **πατρώιος** (nom. sg. masc. adj., "ancestral, hereditary") modifies it; **ἐκ Τάφου** (prep. + gen., "from Taphos") indicates origin; **ἐστίν** (3rd sg. pres. indic. of εἰμί, "is") functions as the copula. The speaker identifies this guest as his ancestral guest-friend who is from Taphos.

lines.original: Μέντης δʼ Ἀγχιάλοιο δαΐφρονος εὔχεται εἶναι
lines.english: He claims to be Mentes son of wise Anchialus and he rules over the oar-loving Taphians.
lines.gloss: **Μέντης** (nom. sg. masc., proper name) "Mentes"; **Ἀγχιάλοιο** (gen. sg. masc., proper name) "of Anchialus"; **δαΐφρονος** (gen. sg. masc., adjective) "warlike, skilled in battle"; **εὔχεται** (3rd sg. pres. mid./pass. indic., εὔχομαι) "claims, professes"; **εἶναι** (pres. act. infin., εἰμί) "to be". Telemachus introduces the disguised Athena as Mentes, claiming to be the son of warlike Anchialus.

lines.original: υἱός, ἀτὰρ Ταφίοισι φιληρέτμοισιν ἀνάσσει.
lines.english: son, and he claims to rule over the oar-loving Taphians.
lines.gloss:
**υἱός** (noun, nominative singular): "son" — Mentor claims to be the son of Anchialus.

**Ταφίοισι** (noun, dative plural): "to/among the Taphians" — the seafaring people over whom Mentor rules.

**φιληρέτμοισιν** (adjective, dative plural): "oar-loving" — epithet describing the Taphians as fond of rowing/seafaring.

**ἀνάσσει** (verb, 3rd singular present): "he rules" — Mentor asserts his lordship over this people.

Athena (disguised as Mentor) completes her false identity by claiming to rule over the seafaring Taphians.

english_paragraphs: Tell me, O Muse, of that many-sided hero who traveled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of. Many cities did he visit, and many were the people with whose customs and thinking [] he was acquainted; many things he suffered at sea while seeking to save his own life [] and to achieve the safe homecoming [] of his companions; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer recklessness in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Helios; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home. Tell me, as you have told those who came before me, about all these things, O daughter of Zeus, starting from whatsoever point you choose.

So now all who escaped death in battle or by shipwreck had got safely home except Odysseus, and he, though he was longing for his return [] to his wife and country, was detained by the goddess Calypso, who had got him into a large cave and wanted to marry him. But as years went by, there came a time when the gods settled that he should go back to; even then, however, when he was among his own people, his trials [] were not yet over; nevertheless all the gods had now begun to pity him except Poseidon, who still persecuted him without ceasing and would not let him get home.

Now Poseidon had gone off to the Ethiopians, who are at the world's end, and lie in two halves, the one looking West and the other East. He had gone there to accept a hecatomb of sheep and oxen, and was enjoying himself at his festival; but the other gods met in the house of Olympian Zeus, and the sire of gods and men spoke first. At that moment he was thinking of Aigisthos, who had been killed by Agamemnon's son Orestes; so he said to the other gods:

"See now, how men consider us gods responsible [] for what is after all nothing but their own folly. Look at Aigisthos; he must needs make love to Agamemnon's wife unrighteously and then kill Agamemnon, though he knew it would be the death of him; for I sent Hermes to warn him not to do either of these things, inasmuch as Orestes would be sure to take his revenge when he grew up and wanted to return home. Hermes told him this in all good will but he would not listen, and now he has paid for everything in full."

Then Athena said, "Father, son of Kronos, King of kings, it served Aigisthos right, and so it would any one else who does as he did; but Aigisthos is neither here nor there; it is for Odysseus that my heart bleeds, when I think of his sufferings in that lonely sea-girt island, far away, poor man, from all his friends. It is an island covered with forest, in the very middle of the sea, and a goddess lives there, daughter of the magician Atlas, who looks after the bottom of the ocean, and carries the great columns that keep heaven and earth asunder. This daughter of Atlas has got hold of poor unhappy Odysseus, and keeps trying by every kind of blandishment to make him forget his home, so that he is tired of life, and thinks of nothing but how he may once more see the smoke of his own chimneys. You, sir, take no heed of this, and yet when Odysseus was beforedid he not propitiate you with many a burnt sacrifice? Why then should you keep on being so angry with him?"

And Zeus said, "My child, what are you talking about? How can I forget Odysseus than whom there is no more capable man on earth, nor more liberal in his offerings to the immortal gods that live in heaven? Bear in mind, however, that Poseidon is still furious with Odysseus for having blinded an eye of Polyphemus king of the Cyclopes. Polyphemus is son to Poseidon by the nymph Thoosa, daughter to the sea-king Phorkys; therefore though he will not kill Odysseus outright, he torments him by preventing him from his homecoming []. Still, let us lay our heads together and see how we can help him to return; Poseidon will then be pacified, for if we are all of a mind he can hardly stand out against us."

And Athena said, "Father, son of Kronos, King of kings, if, then, the gods now mean that Odysseus should get home, we should first send Hermes to the Ogygian island to tell Calypso that we have made up our minds and that he is to have his homecoming []. In the meantime I will go to, to put heart into Odysseus' son Telemakhos; I will embolden him to call the Achaeans in assembly, and speak out to the suitors of his mother Penelope, who persist in eating up any number of his sheep and oxen; I will also conduct him toand to, to see if he can hear anything about the return [] of his dear father - for this will give him genuine fame [] throughout humankind."

So saying she bound on her glittering golden sandals, imperishable, with which she can fly like the wind over land or sea; she grasped the redoubtable bronze-shod spear, so stout and sturdy and strong, wherewith she quells the ranks of heroes who have displeased her, and down she darted from the topmost summits of, whereon forthwith she was in theof, at the gateway of Odysseus' house, disguised as a visitor, Mentes, chief of the Taphians, and she held a bronze spear in her hand. There she found the lordly suitors seated on hides of the oxen which they had killed and eaten, and playing draughts in front of the house. Men-servants and pages were bustling about to wait upon them, some mixing wine with water in the mixing-bowls, some cleaning down the tables with wet sponges and laying them out again, and some cutting up great quantities of meat.

Telemakhos saw her long before any one else did. He was sitting moodily among the suitors thinking about his brave father, and how he would send them fleeing out of the house, if he were to come to his own again and be honored as in days gone by. Thus brooding as he sat among them, he caught sight of Athena and went straight to the gate, for he was vexed that a stranger should be kept waiting for admittance. He took her right hand in his own, and bade her give him her spear. "Welcome," said he, "to our house, and when you have partaken of food you shall tell us what you have come for."

He led the way as he spoke, and Athena followed him. When they were within he took her spear and set it in the spear - stand against a strong bearing-post along with the many other spears of his unhappy father, and he conducted her to a richly decorated seat under which he threw a cloth of damask. There was a footstool also for her feet, and he set another seat near her for himself, away from the suitors, that she might not be annoyed while eating by their noise and insolence, and that he might ask her more freely about his father.

A maid servant then brought them water in a beautiful golden ewer and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands, and she drew a clean table beside them. An upper servant brought them bread, and offered them many good things of what there was in the house, the carver fetched them plates of all manner of meats and set cups of gold by their side, and a man-servant brought them wine and poured it out for them.

Then the suitors came in and took their places on the benches and seats. Forthwith men servants poured water over their hands, maids went round with the bread-baskets, pages filled the mixing-bowls with wine and water, and they laid their hands upon the good things that were before them. As soon as they had had enough to eat and drink they wanted music and dancing, which are the crowning embellishments of a banquet, so a servant brought a lyre to Phemios, whom they compelled perforce to sing to them. As soon as he touched his lyre and began to sing Telemakhos spoke low to Athena, with his head close to hers that no man might hear.

"I hope, sir," said he, "that you will not be offended with what I am going to say. Singing comes cheap to those who do not pay for it, and all this is done at the cost of one whose bones lie rotting in some wilderness or grinding to powder in the surf. If these men were to see my father come back tothey would pray for longer legs rather than a longer purse, for wealth would not serve them; but he, alas, has fallen on an ill fate, and even when people do sometimes say that he is coming, we no longer heed them; we shall never see him again. And now, sir, tell me and tell me true, who you are and where you come from. Tell me of your town and parents, what manner of ship you came in, how your crew brought you to, and of what nation they declared themselves to be - for you cannot have come by land. Tell me also truly, for I want to know, are you a stranger to this house, or have you been here in my father's time? In the old days we had many visitors for my father went about much himself."

And Athena answered, "I will tell you truly and particularly all about it. I am Mentes, son of Anchialos, and I am King of the Taphians. I have come here with my ship and crew, on a voyage to men of a foreign tongue being bound for Temesa with a cargo of iron, and I shall bring back copper. As for my ship, it lies over yonder off the open country away from the town, in the harbor Rheithron under the wooded mountain Neritum. Our fathers were friends before us, as oldwill tell you, if you will go and ask him. They say, however, that he never comes to town now, and lives by himself in the country, faring hardly, with an old woman to look after him and get his dinner for him, when he comes in tired from pottering about his vineyard. They told me your father was at home again, and that was why I came, but it seems the gods are still keeping him back, for he is not dead yet not on the mainland. It is more likely he is on some sea-girt island in mid ocean, or a prisoner among savages who are detaining him against his will. I am no seer [], and know very little about omens, but I speak as it is borne in upon me from heaven, and assure you that he will not be away much longer; for he is a man of such resource that even though he were in chains of iron he would find some means of getting home again. But tell me, and tell me true, can Odysseus really have such a fine looking young man for a son? You are indeed wonderfully like him about the head and eyes, for we were close friends before he set sail forwhere the flower of all the Argives went also. Since that time we have never either of us seen the other."

"My mother," answered Telemakhos, "tells me I am son to Odysseus, but it is a wise child that knows his own father. Would that I were son to one who had grown old upon his own estates, for, since you ask me, there is no more ill-starred man under heaven than he who they tell me is my father."

And Athena said, "There is no fear of your race dying out yet, while Penelope has such a fine son as you are. But tell me, and tell me true, what is the meaning of all this feasting, and who are these people? What is it all about? Have you some banquet, or is there a wedding in the family - for no one seems to be bringing any provisions of his own? And the guests - how atrociously they are behaving; what riot they make over the whole house; it is enough to disgust any respectable person who comes near them."

"Sir," said Telemakhos, "as regards your question, so long as my father was here it was well with us and with the house, but the gods in their displeasure have willed it otherwise, and have hidden him away more closely than mortal man was ever yet hidden. I could have borne it better even though he were dead, if he had fallen with his men in theof, or had died with friends around him when the days of his fighting were done; for then the Achaeans would have built a mound over his ashes, and I should myself have been heir to his renown []; but now the storm-winds have spirited him away we know not wither; he is gone without leaving so much as a trace behind him, and I inherit nothing but dismay. Nor does the matter end simply with grief for the loss of my father; heaven has laid sorrows upon me of yet another kind; for the chiefs from all our islands, Dulichium, Same, and the woodland island of, as also all the principal men ofitself, are eating up my house under the pretext of paying their court to my mother, who will neither point blank say that she will not marry, nor yet bring matters to an end; so they are making havoc of my estate, and before long will do so also with myself."

"Is that so?" exclaimed Athena, "then you do indeed want Odysseus home again. Give him his helmet, shield, and a couple lances, and if he is the man he was when I first knew him in our house, drinking and making merry, he would soon lay his hands about these rascally suitors, were he to stand once more upon his own threshold. He was then coming from, where he had been to beg poison for his arrows from Ilos, son of Mermerus. Ilos feared the ever-living gods and would not give him any, but my father let him have some, for he was very fond of him. If Odysseus is the man he then was these suitors will have a swift doom and a sorry wedding.

"But there! It rests with heaven to determine whether he is to return, and take his revenge in his own house or no; I would, however, urge you to set about trying to get rid of these suitors at once. Take my advice, call the Achaean heroes in assembly tomorrow -lay your case before them, and call heaven to bear you witness. Bid the suitors take themselves off, each to his own place, and if your mother's mind is set on marrying again, let her go back to her father, who will find her a husband and provide her with all the marriage gifts that so dear a daughter may expect. As for yourself, let me prevail upon you to take the best ship you can get, with a crew of twenty men, and go in quest of your father who has so long been missing. Some one may tell you something, or (and people often hear things in this way) some heaven-sent message [] may direct you. First go toand ask Nestor; thence go on toand visit Menelaos, for he got home last of all the Achaeans; if you hear that your father is alive and about to achieve his homecoming [], you can put up with the waste these suitors will make for yet another twelve months. If on the other hand you hear of his death, come home at once, celebrate his funeral rites with all due pomp, build a grave marker [] to his memory, and make your mother marry again. Then, having done all this, think it well over in your mind how, by fair means or foul, you may kill these suitors in your own house. You are too old to plead infancy any longer; have you not heard how people are singing Orestes' praises [] for having killed his father's murderer Aigisthos? You are a fine, smart looking young man; show your mettle, then, and make yourself a name in story. Now, however, I must go back to my ship and to my crew, who will be impatient if I keep them waiting longer; think the matter over for yourself, and remember what I have said to you."

"Sir," answered Telemakhos, "it has been very kind of you to talk to me in this way, as though I were your own son, and I will do all you tell me; I know you want to be getting on with your voyage, but stay a little longer till you have taken a bath and refreshed yourself. I will then give you a present, and you shall go on your way rejoicing; I will give you one of great beauty and value - a keepsake such as only dear friends give to one another."

Athena answered, "Do not try to keep me, for I would be on my way at once. As for any present you may be disposed to make me, keep it till I come again, and I will take it home with me. You shall give me a very good one, and I will give you one of no less value in return."

With these words she flew away like a bird into the air, but she had given Telemakhos courage, and had made him think more than ever about his father. He felt the change, wondered at it, and knew that the stranger had been a god, so he went straight to where the suitors were sitting.

Phemios was still singing, and his hearers sat rapt in silence as he told the baneful tale of the homecoming [] from, and the ills Athena had laid upon the Achaeans. Penelope, daughter of Ikarios, heard his song from her room upstairs, and came down by the great staircase, not alone, but attended by two of her handmaids. When she reached the suitors she stood by one of the bearing posts that supported the roof of the cloisters with a staid maiden on either side of her. She held a veil, moreover, before her face, and was weeping bitterly.

"Phemios," she cried, "you know many another feat of gods and heroes, such as poets love to celebrate. Sing the suitors some one of these, and let them drink their wine in silence, but cease this sad tale, for it breaks my sorrowful heart, and reminds me of my lost husband for whom I have grief [] ever without ceasing, and whose name [] was great over alland middle."

"Mother," answered Telemakhos, "let the bard sing what he has a mind [] to; bards are not responsible [] for the ills they sing of; it is Zeus, not they, who is responsible [], and who sends weal or woe upon humankind according to his own good pleasure. There should be no feeling ofagainst this one for singing the ill-fated return of the Danaans, for people always favor most warmly theof the latest songs. Make up your mind to it and bear it; Odysseus is not the only man who never came back from, but many another went down as well as he. Go, then, within the house and busy yourself with your daily duties, your loom, your distaff, and the ordering of your servants; for speech is man's matter, and mine above all others - for it is I who am master here."

She went wondering back into the house, and laid her son's saying in her heart. Then, going upstairs with her handmaids into her room, she mourned her dear husband till Athena shed sweet sleep over her eyes. But the suitors were clamorous throughout the covered cloisters, and prayed each one that he might be her bed fellow.

Then Telemakhos spoke, "You suitors of my mother," he cried, "you with your overweening, let us feast at our pleasure now, and let there be no brawling, for it is a rare thing to hear a man with such a divine voice as Phemios has; but in the morning meet me in full assembly that I may give you formal notice to depart, and feast at one another's houses, turn and turn about, at your own cost. If on the other hand you choose to persist in sponging upon one man, heaven help me, but Zeus shall reckon with you in full, and when you fall in my father's house there shall be no man to avenge you."

The suitors bit their lips as they heard him, and marveled at the boldness of his speech. Then, Antinoos, son of Eupeithes, said, "The gods seem to have given you lessons in bluster and tall talking; may Zeus never grant you to be chief inas your father was before you."

Telemakhos answered, "Antinoos, do not chide with me, but, god willing, I will be chief too if I can. Is this the worst fate you can think of for me? It is no bad thing to be a chief, for it brings both riches and honor. Still, now that Odysseus is dead there are many great men inboth old and young, and some other may take the lead among them; nevertheless I will be chief in my own house, and will rule those whom Odysseus has won for me."

Then Eurymakhos, son of Polybos, answered, "It rests with heaven to decide who shall be chief among us, but you shall be master in your own house and over your own possessions; no one while there is a man inshall do you violence [] nor rob you. And now, my good man, I want to know about this stranger. What country does he come from? Of what family is he, and where is his estate? Has he brought you news about the return of your father, or was he on business of his own? He seemed a well-to-do man, but he hurried off so suddenly that he was gone in a moment before we could get to know him."

"Theof my father is dead and gone," answered Telemakhos, "and even if some rumor reaches me I put no more faith in it now. My mother does indeed sometimes send for a soothsayer and question him, but I give his prophesying no heed. As for the stranger, he was Mentes, son of Anchialos, chief of the Taphians, an old friend of my father's." But in his heart he knew that it had been the goddess.

The suitors then returned to their singing and dancing until the evening; but when night fell upon their pleasuring they went home to bed each in his own abode. Telemakhos' room was high up in a tower that looked on to the outer court; there, then, he went, brooding and full of thought. A good old woman, Eurykleia, daughter of Ops, the son of Pisenor, went before him with a couple of blazing torches.had bought her with his own wealth when she was quite young; he gave the worth of twenty oxen for her, and showed as much respect to her in his household as he did to his own wedded wife, but he did not take her to his bed for he feared his wife's resentment. She it was who now lighted Telemakhos to his room, and she loved him better than any of the other women in the house did, for she had nursed him when he was a baby. He opened the door of his bed room and sat down upon the bed; as he took off his shirt he gave it to the good old woman, who folded it tidily up, and hung it for him over a peg by his bed side, after which she went out, pulled the door to by a silver catch, and drew the bolt home by means of the strap. But Telemakhos as he lay covered with a woolen fleece kept thinking all night through of his intended voyage and of the counsel that Athena had given him.
